title: The Cradle of the Void
mood: Obsidia finds the one place Vexana thought was hers, then leads her to where the Enders are made.

hero.alt: Obsidia looks back over her shoulder under a dark violet sky, a faint smile on her face and a pink star glowing at her chest.

segs.t: The feeders went off into the dark with the night’s girders. Vexana had never followed them. She turned the other way, toward the hollow.
Her fingers were already at the cuff of her right sleeve. In the hollow she always bared the star.
Then she saw a glow there.
Among her Guards, where no light but hers had ever burned, a pink star was shining.
It sat at the chest of a black-and-magenta gown. Obsidia hung before the lead Guard with her clawed glove laid flat on its heart. By her light, gold showed along the edges of its purple plate.
Under the glove the heart stayed dark. So did the eyes.
Vexana stopped short in the dark. The cuff slid out of her fingers.
Her eyes went straight to the folded uniform. The pink-haired keychain still lay on top of it.
The one place,
she thought.
The one place nothing comes.
Every plate in those four she had carried home in a sack. Every joint she had beaten until it caught.
She did not touch them. She only wanted them lit.
The lead Guard’s eyes came on, yellow. A hum started in its chest, and its heart blazed magenta under Obsidia’s palm. Behind it the three giants lit one after another. Their swords came up.
Obsidia did not take her hand away. She looked up into the yellow eyes.
“What intriguing technology,” she said.
Nothing moved. Three swords hung in the air over Obsidia’s head.
“Our plate. Our cores.” Her palm stayed on the blazing heart. “Dead under my hand, and they stand up for you.”
“Step away from it,” said Vexana.
Obsidia took her glove from the heart without hurry, and turned.
Her eyes went over the folded uniform and the little keychain on it. They moved on.
Vexana kept her own eyes on Obsidia, and waited for the question.
What are they for?
It did not come.
Four machines, built to stand against the body. To its commander they were not worth asking about.
Either she thinks they change nothing,
Vexana thought.
Or she wants to see what they do.
“How did you find this place?”
“I marked this fold the night my ship came through.”
How, Obsidia did not say.
A self found it,
Vexana thought.
She kept the star to herself. She will keep this.
No eyes from the rows have been in here. To the Will I am still the one who fetches its metal.
She let the Guards go dark, one after another. The swords sank back down.
“Twice you went to the rows,” said Obsidia. “Twice you kept to their edge.”
So the eyes in the rows had seen her, and Obsidia had read them.
“You have never looked where they are made. Come.”
Vexana looked once more at her dark Guards.
Better her eyes on the rows than here,
she thought.
Obsidia moved off into the dark. Vexana went beside her.
There was nothing under them and nothing over them. The only light was Obsidia’s star and, far ahead, the faint violet of the rows.
“Our teacher said nobody can get near this dark,” said Vexana. Under a shady tree she had said it herself, with Guinevere’s head in her lap.
“Your teacher was right.” Obsidia did not look back. “Every door into it opens from this side. The Will opens them. I open my own.”
“Who opens mine?”
“It does, where it sends you. No device of your people’s opens one from outside. So your people never come.”
“I came.”
“You were brought.”
Ahead, the violet of the rows grew. Nothing in it moved.
“How long do they wait there?” said Vexana.
“Some, for ages. The dark slows whatever waits in it. They need nothing.”
On errand nights Vexana ate from tins in dead kitchens, and not many. Weeks in this dark, and she had hardly been hungry. Now she knew why.
“What is it?” she said. “This dark.”
“What there was before Balance. Everything returns to it at the end, and begins from it again.”
“You’ve seen that?”
“No one has.”
“Then it’s a grave.”
“A cradle,” said Obsidia.
In the nest the rows ran on past sight. Gray Enders lay in them by the thousand, side by side, still.
Every one of them had eyes. Vexana kept a step behind Obsidia.
An instrument at its commander’s heel,
she thought.
Nothing for the Will to notice.
Under the rows the dark turned soft. Purple tissue spread there like roots, out from the body’s vast flank far above. Each Ender lay sunk in it to the shoulders.
Out of habit she searched the rows for the Core. She found rows.
At the near end, tissue hung down out of the dark in long purple ropes. At the end of one, a shape was swelling, slow.
Metal drifted in to it out of the dark, girders and plate. Where the metal touched the tissue it glowed red and bent. Piece by piece it closed over the shape into a shell.
One girder still had a bracket bolted to it, the kind that held up a balcony.
Hours ago she had watched feeders tear girders like that one out of fallen houses.
So this is where it goes,
she thought.
Every house it breaks comes back as one of them.
She said nothing.
Obsidia went on along the rows. The shells grew as they went: twice the height of the gray ones, then as tall as towers. In the largest the chest stood open, and smaller shapes lay folded inside.
“Enders,” said Vexana. “Super Enders. Ultimate Enders.”
“The large ones carry the others in,” said Obsidia. “They let them out where the fighting is.”
“Where is your row?”
“There is no row for me.”
“When we kill one,” said Vexana, “what happens to it?”
“Its core breaks.” Obsidia laid a claw on a gray shell as she passed. “The Will’s thread in it snaps, and the Will feels it. When too many snap at once, the wound is more than it can carry.”
Vexana saw Chang’e’s screen again, the row of jagged lines, every one stopping in the same moment.
Something switches them all off at once,
Chang’e had said.
That was the Will,
Vexana thought.
Hurt.
“And the dead?” she said. “Where do they go?”
“I do not know where they go.” Obsidia turned her head. “Do you know where yours go?”
Vexana thought of her father’s toolbox, set down beside her cot in the Shield’s home. It was all of him that had come back to her.
She kept walking.
Past the largest shells lay a short row, apart from the rest. Its shells were not gray.
They had faces.
Human faces, smooth, with the eyes shut. Some were no bigger than a child. One had hands, folded. One was split open down the front, from the inside, and nothing was in it.
Vexana’s skin crawled under her armor.
“Mine,” said Obsidia. “I shaped them toward your likeness. Some broke when the body first moved them. None of them held a self.”
“Why make them like us?”
Obsidia looked down at the faces.
“If we are the instruments of their destruction, why were we made so much in their likeness?” she said.
Vexana looked at the one asking it. A woman’s face. A hand inside a glove.
She had no answer either.
At the end of the row the tissue was pressed into one more shape, small and curled, no longer than the smallest shell. Nothing lay in it.
Obsidia stopped there. Her clawed glove rested on the edge of the dent, and stayed.
She said nothing about it.
One more that broke,
Vexana thought.
Cleared away.
Obsidia took her hand from the edge and turned to her.
“I have asked the body,” she said. “It has no after to answer with. I have never asked one of you.”
Vexana waited.
“Once humanity has been purged, what will become of us?” Obsidia asked.
Now Obsidia waited. The rows lay still around them.
Pink broke open in Vexana’s memory, then gold, over dark grass at the dome’s edge. A face below it, lit a new color by every burst.
“Someone told me once that we’d be like fireworks,” she said.
“Fireworks.”
“Shining at our brightest.”
“And after the fireworks?”
Vexana thought about it. “She never said.”
Obsidia’s eyes went out along the rows. “Fireworks,” she said. “Then dark.”
For me, then dark,
Vexana thought.
Not for her.
“What is yours?” she said at last.

“I know two,” said Obsidia. “After the last people I helped end, we slept here for ages, until the host grew a new people. I have also watched Enders with nothing left to kill. They turned on each other, until the body unmade what was left.”
“Which will it be?”
“That is what I mean to find out.” Her eyes went back along the row of faces.
“Suppose one held,” said Vexana. “A self, in our likeness.”
Obsidia kept her eyes on the faces.
“The Will lets a pawn move freely for a while,” she said. “A small taste of freedom. If it ever slips beyond control, there is only one outcome.”
“Termination,” said Vexana.
Obsidia inclined her head.
Vexana’s left hand had gone to her right sleeve, to the pin under the cloth. She took it away.
Free for a while,
she thought.
Until the day it finds out.
“Has one ever held?” she said.
Obsidia moved to the end of the rows. Far off past them hung the crack of human sky.
“I have watched many worlds,” she said. “On a dead one, under a gray sky, I saw the body come through a door. Over another city six stars opened, and nothing was left standing.”

media.alt: On a dead gray world under a dark sky, a winged woman raises one hand as red stars burn open overhead; then red four-pointed stars open in a storm sky over a city of towers, and the city vanishes in a blinding pink blast.

segs.t: She was quiet for a moment.
“And once, among a people in the rain, I set down a seed with my own hands. The first of my making to hold a perfect human form.”
Another world,
Vexana thought.
Another people she ended.
“Of all I have made, she is the finest.” Obsidia’s voice did not change. “She does not answer when I call.”
Even what she makes says no to her,
Vexana thought.
Obsidia looked up past the rows, toward the crack.
“When the final stage arrives, I hope she will finally understand her purpose,” she said.
She stayed so, her face turned up to it. On the other side of the crack, rain was running down the human sky.
